n: Beyond the Twelve, Jesus appoints seventy more and sends them in pairs ahead of Him to prepare towns for His visit. Only Luke records this mission. The Church today still has quorums of the Seventy who serve under the Twelve.

f.g: Some early manuscripts read seventy-two. The number recalls the seventy elders who helped Moses.

n: There are many people ready to receive the gospel but few workers to gather them. Jesus asks the disciples to pray for more laborers — and then sends them as an answer to that very prayer.
They go out vulnerable, like lambs surrounded by wolves. Their safety will come from God, not from their own strength.
No money bag, no supply sack, no extra sandals — and no long roadside greetings. The mission is urgent, and they must rely fully on the Lord.

f.w: salute no man by the way
f.g: Eastern greetings could involve lengthy ceremonies; they were not to be delayed by social formalities.
A traveler’s food bag.

n: Their first words on entering a home are to be a blessing of peace — the common Jewish greeting “Shalom,” now carrying the peace of the gospel.
If someone receptive lives there, the blessing of peace will rest on that home. If not, the blessing comes back to the missionaries — nothing is wasted.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for a person of peace, someone open to it.

n: They are to stay in the same house and accept whatever food is offered. Those who labor in the Lord’s work may rightly receive support from those they serve.

f.w: the labourer is worthy of his hire
Go not from house to house
f.g: Don’t move around seeking better accommodations.

n: In welcoming towns, they should gratefully eat what is served — without fussing over food customs.

f.w: eat such things as are set before you

n: They are to heal the sick and announce that God’s kingdom has drawn near. Healing shows the kingdom’s power; preaching explains it.

f.g: Near.

n: If a town refuses them, they are to go out into its streets and make a public declaration.
Wiping off the town’s dust is a solemn witness that they bear no responsibility for the town’s choice. Yet even in rejection, the message stands: the kingdom came near.

f.g: Clings, sticks.

n: Sodom was notorious for wickedness, yet it never had the chance these towns had. Those who reject greater light carry greater accountability.

f.g: More bearable.

n: Jesus mourns over Galilean towns where He had done many miracles. Even the pagan cities of Tyre and Sidon would have repented long ago had they seen what these towns saw.

f.g: A town just north of Capernaum.
Rough goat-hair clothing and ashes on the head — signs of grief and repentance.

n: On Judgment Day, these Gentile cities will fare better than the towns that saw Jesus’ works and still refused Him.

f.g: Ancient Phoenician seaports on the Mediterranean coast north of Galilee.

n: Capernaum, Jesus’ home base, had been lifted up by His presence — yet in its pride it would be brought down. Its ruins today stand as a quiet witness.

f.g: Greek hadēs, the world of departed spirits; here the depths, the opposite of heaven.

n: To hear Christ’s authorized servants is to hear Christ, and to reject them is to reject Him and His Father. The authority of the messenger comes from the One who sends.

f.w: He that heareth you heareth me

n: The seventy return thrilled: even evil spirits obeyed them in Jesus’ name.
Jesus sees their success as part of Satan’s defeat. Satan was cast out of heaven long ago, and now his power on earth is being broken.

f.w: I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven

n: Jesus gives them authority over every power of the enemy — symbolized by snakes and scorpions. Nothing will be able to defeat them spiritually.
Still, power over spirits is not the true reason for joy. The greater joy is having one’s name recorded in heaven — belonging to God forever.

f.w: your names are written in heaven

n: Jesus overflows with joy and thanks the Father that heavenly truths have been revealed to the humble and childlike, while those proud of their learning miss them.

f.g: Little children — here the humble and teachable.

f.w: hid these things from the wise and prudent

n: The Father has given all things to the Son. Only the Father fully knows the Son, and only the Son fully knows the Father — and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.

f.w: he to whom the Son will reveal him

n: Privately, Jesus tells His disciples how blessed they are to witness these things.

f.w: Blessed are the eyes which see

n: Prophets and kings of old longed to see the Messiah’s day, but only saw it from afar. The disciples are living what generations looked forward to.

f.w: many prophets and kings have desired to see

n: An expert in the law of Moses tests Jesus with the most important question anyone can ask: how do I gain eternal life?

f.g: Not a courtroom attorney but a scholar of the law of Moses.
Tested.

n: Jesus turns the question back: You know the law — what does it say? How do you read it?

f.g: How do you interpret it?

n: The lawyer answers well, combining two commandments: love God completely (from Deuteronomy) and love your neighbor as yourself (from Leviticus).

f.w: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God

n: Jesus agrees: correct answer. Now live it, and you will have life. Knowing isn’t enough — doing is what matters.

f.w: this do, and thou shalt live

n: Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer looks for a limit: exactly who counts as my neighbor? He hopes to narrow his obligation.

f.g: Make himself look right.

n: Jesus tells a story. The steep road from Jerusalem down to Jericho dropped about 3,000 feet through rocky, lonely country and was known for bandits. A traveler is robbed, beaten, and left for dead.

f.w: went down from Jerusalem to Jericho
f.g: About 17 miles, descending from about 2,500 feet above sea level to about 800 feet below.
Clothing.

n: A priest comes by — someone who served at the temple. He sees the man and deliberately crosses to the other side. Perhaps he feared ritual defilement from a possible corpse, or simply didn’t want the trouble.

f.w: passed by on the other side

n: A Levite, a temple assistant, does the same — looking at the man, then passing by. Religious standing did not produce compassion.

f.g: A member of the tribe of Levi who assisted the priests in temple service.

n: The hero is a Samaritan — someone Jews of that day despised. Moved with compassion, he stops. Jesus deliberately makes the outsider the example.

f.g: Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility; the lawyer would never expect him to be the hero.

n: He treats the wounds with oil to soothe and wine to disinfect, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and cares for him through the night. Many early Christians saw Christ Himself in this rescuer.

f.g: Common first-aid of the day: olive oil soothed; wine cleansed.
His pack animal, likely a donkey.

n: The next day he pays the innkeeper two denarii — about two days’ wages — and promises to cover anything more when he returns. His mercy is generous and lasting.

f.g: Two denarii; a denarius was a typical day’s wage for a laborer.

f.w: when I come again, I will repay thee
f.g: Many readers see a hint of Christ’s promised return.

n: Jesus flips the lawyer’s question. Not “who is my neighbor?” but “who acted as a neighbor?” The question is not whom we must love, but whether we will love.

f.g: Being a neighbor is an action, not a category.

n: The lawyer can’t bring himself to say “the Samaritan,” but he gives the right answer: the one who showed mercy. Jesus’ command is simple: go and do the same.
Jesus enters a village — John tells us it was Bethany near Jerusalem — and Martha welcomes Him into her home.
Her sister Mary sits at Jesus’ feet listening to Him — the posture of a disciple. Remarkably, Jesus welcomes a woman as a student of His teaching.

f.g: The traditional position of a student before a rabbi.

n: Martha is overwhelmed by all the work of hosting and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help. Her service is good, but she has become anxious and resentful.

f.g: Distracted, pulled in many directions.

n: Jesus speaks to her tenderly, repeating her name. He sees that she is anxious and upset about so many things.

f.g: Full of care — anxious, worried.

n: Only one thing is truly necessary: drawing near to Him. Mary has chosen the best part, and Jesus will not take it from her. Service matters, but never at the cost of being with the Lord.

f.g: The best portion, as in the choice share of a meal.
